beliefs.practice: Enforce idempotency by creating a unique index on the transactionRef field but only for documents that include it (createIndex({ transactionRef: 1 }, { unique: true, partialFilterExpression: { transactionRef: { $exists: true } } })) so multiple legacy/missing-ref documents are allowed.

Use multi-document transactions with explicit sessions: start a session, startTransaction({ readConcern: 'snapshot', writeConcern: { w: 'majority' } }), perform Transaction insert and Account update using the same session, then commitTransaction/abort as needed; treat commit errors labeled UnknownTransactionCommitResult/TransientTransactionError according to MongoDB retry flow.

Store money in a non-floating type: use Decimal128 (mongoose.Schema.Types.Decimal128) or integer minor-units (cents) for amount fields to avoid rounding errors and maintain consistent comparison/index behavior.

Create a compound index to support efficient account transaction queries, e.g. createIndex({ accountId: 1, createdAt: -1 }), so queries that fetch recent transactions for an account use an index and avoid collection scans.

Create indexes at startup (model.createIndexes()) and fail fast on index creation errors rather than relying on background/implicit creation during traffic; ensure your deployment/CI runs index creation once before production traffic.

Do not auto-retry the whole transaction blindly on any error; only retry when the driver marks the error as TransientTransactionError or on UnknownTransactionCommitResult with the documented MongoDB retry/commit pattern, and implement exponential backoff with a small max retry count.

Reuse a single Mongoose connection across the app (singleton) and configure pool options (e.g. maxPoolSize) via the connection string or Mongoose options; avoid opening/closing connections per request.

Keep transactions short and touch as few documents as possible—do the minimum update to the account snapshot plus the append insert—to reduce lock contention and RU consumption; avoid long-running business logic inside a transaction.

Use a snapshot-style ledger design: immutable Transaction documents for each debit/credit and a separate Account snapshot document for fast reads/aggregates; only update the Account snapshot in the transaction, never mutate historical Transaction documents.

Read DOCUMENTDB_URI from environment (process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI) and never commit credentials to source control; provide a .env.example with a placeholder and recommend storing the real secret in Azure Key Vault or environment variables managed by the hosting environment.

When creating the unique transactionRef index, use a partial index or sparse:true to avoid a uniqueness constraint on documents without transactionRef (unique:false behavior for nulls is not safe); verify index behavior by inserting test docs before running production traffic.

Use proper numeric comparison types in queries and updates (Decimal128 or integers) and ensure Mongoose casts values correctly when using $inc on balances; avoid floating-point $inc on Number fields for money.

Monitor RU/s consumption and index usage via Azure monitoring; provision either adequate manual RU or use autoscale to prevent request rate throttling, because transactions and large read/writes increase RU cost.

Avoid storing large binary/blobs or large vectors in the ledger documents themselves; if vector search is used, store vectors in a dedicated collection with its own vector index (HNSW/IVF) and tune index params (M, efConstruction, efSearch) separate from transactional collections.

Use server-side validators / Mongoose schema validation to enforce required fields (accountId, amount, transactionRef, createdAt, type) and types, and treat schema validation as a first-line defense against malformed ledger writes.

When updating the Account snapshot inside the transaction, use an atomic $inc for balance (with Decimal128 or integer cents) and use options that return the updated document if needed (findOneAndUpdate with { session, returnDocument: 'after' } in Mongoose/driver) to avoid race conditions.

Handle duplicate-key errors (E11000) explicitly in the API flow as evidence of a repeated idempotent request; translate those to idempotent success (200/202) or to a clear 409 that includes the existing transaction id rather than retrying the insertion.

Test and verify indexes and query plans against the actual cluster (use the provided documentdb MCP server or explain()) after index creation to confirm queries are using the indexes you expect and not triggering full scans.

Design the partitioning / shard key (or logical partition key) with accountId as a leading key to keep all an account's transactions co-located and to avoid cross-partition transactions when possible; verify the provider's partitioning model and limits before assuming cross-partition transactions are cheap.

Keep detailed immutable audit metadata on each Transaction (createdAt, createdBy, transactionRef, source, idempotency metadata) so you can reconcile duplicates and debug failed commits without relying on mutable history.

Avoid TTL indexes on ledger/transaction collections (do not create createIndex({ createdAt: 1 }, { expireAfterSeconds: ... })) because ledgers should be durable and immutable; if you must expire data, keep it in a separate non-ledger collection.

Use Azure-native secret stores (Key Vault) and role-based identity for host services rather than embedding DB credentials in code or container images; rotate credentials periodically and test connection string renewals in a staging environment.

Instrument and emit metrics for transaction commit failures, retry counts, E11000 duplicates, RU/throughput throttling responses, and slow queries; wire these into Azure Monitor/Prometheus so you can detect operational issues early.

When using Mongoose, pass the session object explicitly to all Model/Document operations inside a transaction (Model.create([...], { session }), Model.findOneAndUpdate(filter, update, { session })), and be cautious with Mongoose middleware that may spawn operations outside the session.
